options: Entire rows -- you cannot delete only part of a row
Only the columns listed after DELETE
The table structure along with its data
Only rows that have NULL in every column
questions.explain: DELETE FROM never names columns -- it removes whole matching rows, not individual column values.

questions.q: What happens when you run 'DELETE FROM dbo.LessonDemo;' with no WHERE clause?
options: Every row in the table is removed, but the table structure remains
SQL Server requires a WHERE clause and raises a syntax error
Only the first row is removed
The table itself is dropped
questions.explain: Just like UPDATE, omitting WHERE in a DELETE applies it to every row -- the empty table itself, its columns and constraints, still exist afterward.

questions.q: Why is it good practice to run a matching SELECT before running a DELETE with the same condition?
options: DELETE is permanent and has no built-in preview, so the SELECT confirms exactly which rows will disappear
SQL Server requires a SELECT to run immediately before every DELETE
It automatically restores deleted rows if something goes wrong
It is required to compute SCOPE_IDENTITY() afterward
questions.explain: Since a DELETE doesn't show you the rows before removing them, previewing with the identical WHERE condition is the best protection against deleting the wrong rows.

questions.q: In 'DELETE d FROM dbo.LessonDemo AS d JOIN Production.Product AS p ON d.ProductName = p.Name WHERE p.ProductLine <> 'R';', what determines which rows are deleted?
options: Rows in dbo.LessonDemo whose matching product's ProductLine is not 'R'
Every row in Production.Product regardless of ProductLine
Only rows with no match in Production.Product
Rows where ProductName is NULL
questions.explain: The join finds matching product names, and WHERE further restricts the delete to rows whose matched product is outside the 'R' line.

questions.q: In a joined DELETE statement, what goes right after the DELETE keyword?
options: The table alias, the same way UPDATE uses an alias right after UPDATE
The WHERE clause
The literal table name only, never an alias
The JOIN keyword
questions.explain: DELETE <alias> FROM <table> AS <alias> JOIN ... mirrors the UPDATE <alias> SET ... FROM ... JOIN ... pattern from the previous lesson.
